name: Zapatismo
summary: Zapatismo is the agrarian revolutionary outlook of Emiliano Zapata and the Liberation Army of the South in the Mexican Revolution. It held that land, water and woods taken by haciendas must be restored to the villages and that great estates must be broken up so every family can farm its own plot, communally or as small property. Around that core its intellectuals drafted a social state: recognition of unions and strikes, labour protections, public assistance as justice, municipal self-government, popular juries, plebiscites on laws and an armed people in place of a standing army.
scope: Emiliano Zapata's own Zapatismo, 1911-1919: the Plan of Ayala (1911), the Liberation Army of the South, the Morelos agrarian reform and 'commune' of 1914-1916, the Agrarian Law of 1915 and the other laws of the Zapatista-led Executive Council of the Convention (1915-1916), and Zapata's letters such as his 1918 letter on the Russian revolution, read with the historians cited (Ávila Espinosa, building on Womack, Rueda and others). Where the council's intellectuals went beyond what the movement practised (gradual socialisation, laicism, divorce), answers are lower confidence. It excludes the EZLN and 1990s neozapatismo, audited separately as neozapatismo.

keyFigures.name: Emiliano Zapata
keyFigures.role: Leader of the Liberation Army of the South and namesake of the ideology; signer of the Plan of Ayala.

keyFigures.name: Otilio Montaño
keyFigures.role: Co-author of the Plan of Ayala and the movement's main early intellectual; later in charge of public instruction.

keyFigures.name: Manuel Palafox
keyFigures.role: Zapatista secretary of agriculture who directed the Morelos land reform and drafted the 1915 Agrarian Law.

sources.title: Plan of Ayala
sources.author: Emiliano Zapata, Otilio Montaño et al. (1911), trans. John Womack Jr.
sources.usedFor: Repudiation of Madero, armed revolution, land restitution, one-third expropriation, nationalisation of opponents' property, Juárez's Church-property laws as model, elections after victory, 'principles not men'.

sources.title: Letter on the Russian Revolution (14 February 1918, to Jenaro Amezcua)
sources.author: Emiliano Zapata (translated by taller ahuehuete)
sources.usedFor: Land as common property like water and air, landlord exploitation, worker-peasant unity, internationalism and the Russian revolution.

sources.usedFor: 1915 Agrarian Law, labour law, unions and strikes in the Convention programme, justice and death penalty, public assistance, officials' morality, army abolition, education, marriage, taxes, plebiscite, parliamentary regime and Senate abolition, municipal autonomy.

sources.usedFor: Bottom-up municipal land decisions, cooperatives and credit unions, nationalised industry, Nahua communal land background.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The Zapatista labour law set a minimum wage fixed yearly by local revolutionary reform boards, showing support for wage floors set to protect workers.

unions-good.rationale: Zapatista delegates at the Convention won votes, against the Villistas, to give legal recognition to workers' organisations, strikes and boycotts.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Plan of Ayala ordered one-third of large estates expropriated and the whole property of opponents nationalised, treating landed property as overridable for justice.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Zapatista law made employers liable for accidents, set an eight-hour day and minimum wages, and allowed socialising harmful monopolies, which amounts to tighter control of business.

cut-welfare.rationale: The Zapatista public-assistance law made the state responsible for feeding, housing and caring for everyone unable to work, as a matter of justice rather than charity.

worker-ownership.rationale: The 1915 labour law aimed at the gradual socialisation of production through workers' cooperatives, though Ávila notes the wider movement never practised this; support is a leadership position.

strong-leader.rationale: The Plan of Ayala declares its authors 'partisans of principles and not of men' and repudiates Madero's personal rule, rejecting a leader above the law.

state-harmful.rationale: Despite anarchist influences on its slogans, Zapatismo set out to take power and build a new social state that guarantees land and labour rights, so it did not reject the state.

empower-police-military.rationale: The Zapatista council called the standing army 'an instrument of murder' used to oppress the people and legislated to abolish it.

decide-locally.rationale: The movement restored the authority of the pueblos and municipal autonomy and relied on municipalities to carry out reforms, though it kept agrarian reform under a central ministry.

rehabilitation.rationale: The Zapatista justice law held society responsible for crime and set up agricultural and industrial regeneration centres to rehabilitate offenders through work.

traditional-family.rationale: The village base was Catholic and traditional, while the leadership's marriage law recognised free unions and gave natural children equal rights; the two pull in opposite directions.

gradual-change.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls Mexicans to take up arms, seize stolen lands at once and accept no compromise with the old regime.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: No international body existed to take a view on; the movement neither sought nor rejected one, so the answer is a neutral inference.

free-trade.rationale: The council wanted free trade in basic necessities while fostering national industry and opposing foreign investment, a mixed stance on trade.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The council wanted technical education and experimental farm stations, but its core problem was land monopoly, not technology; a neutral inference.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls on Mexicans to support it 'with arms in hand' and pledges to continue the revolution until victory or death.

experts-over-public.rationale: Zapatista justice law sought to end lawyers' 'monopoly' of justice through popular juries, and laws were to be ratified by plebiscite, favouring the public over specialists.

land-value-tax.rationale: Mendoza López blamed ground rent for poverty, a Georgist-like idea, but the movement chose expropriation and restitution rather than a land tax.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The programme wanted to foster national industry yet also free trade in necessities; its stance on tariffs is unclear.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Zapatista plans had the agriculture ministry finance an agricultural bank, regional farm schools and experiment stations, and proposed a state bank to develop national industry.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The 1915 agrarian law gave every person a natural right to land for their family, capped holdings, and gave communal and small private property equal legal standing.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Zapatista finance proposals included a state bank and monetary unification, the opposite of leaving money to the market.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Local reform boards set minimum wages and settled labour disputes, a state-recognised body, but not a joint employer-worker corporation; the fit is unclear.

democracy-best.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls for elections to federal and state powers after victory, and the council held that real democracy means voters approve laws as well as choose rulers.

direct-votes.rationale: A council law required the fundamental laws of the republic to be ratified by plebiscite, defining real democracy as approving or rejecting laws by popular vote.

right-to-secede.rationale: The Plan of Ayala invokes state sovereignty against Madero, but the movement sought a national government; secession was never discussed.

political-violence-never.rationale: Zapatismo was an armed movement whose founding plan orders villages to hold recovered land by force of arms.

separate-church-state.rationale: The council's education law made primary schooling lay, and the Plan models itself on Juárez's Reform laws; Ávila notes laicism was the intellectuals' view more than the base's.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Zapata's 1918 letter frames history as the awakening of oppressed peoples against exploiting landlords and warns of the bourgeoisie, a class reading though not a Marxist one.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The Plan of Ayala restores land, woods and water to villages holding title to them, many of them Nahua communities that had held land in common.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Zapata likened foreign capital to Spanish colonial extraction but never asked Spain for reparations; the question does not map onto the movement.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The movement spoke both of natural rights to land and of strict duties of revolutionary morality; neither clearly comes first.

restore-past-order.rationale: Recent historians reject the old view that Zapatismo only wanted to restore a golden age of village peace, yet restitution of lost lands was central.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Zapata's own headquarters governed pragmatically while the intellectuals wrote programmes; there is no stated view on this.

direct-action.rationale: The Plan of Ayala tells villages to take immediate possession of stolen land, rather than wait for courts or legislatures, though it also planned elections.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Ávila describes a natural division of labour within the movement between farmers, soldiers and intellectuals; abolition was never sought.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Mendoza López counted industrialists and merchants among the productive classes and singled out only landlords as idle exploiters, so profit as such was not condemned.

collective-farming.rationale: The Zapatista agrarian law gave communal and individual holdings equal legal status and left each community and person free to choose either.

taxation-theft.rationale: The council restructured taxes and wanted heavy taxes on foreign firms, so it accepted taxation; it did call taxes on necessities and on labour obstacles to be removed.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The agrarian law recognised the rights of communities as well as individuals to restored land and to choose communal tenure.

positive-liberty.rationale: Zapatismo held that freedom required land for subsistence: the agrarian law made the state guarantee each person's natural right to the land they need.

organic-representation.rationale: Zapatista practice relied on village and municipal councils, yet its programme also kept direct suffrage and a parliament; the fit is unclear.

bound-labor.rationale: Zapatismo rose against the hacienda system that tied peons to estates, and its agrarian law gave tenants and sharecroppers the land they worked.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The sources contain no epistemological view; the justice law did say courts had served the powerful, which is not the same claim.

universal-morality.rationale: The Zapatista justice law describes laws as expressions of 'eternal and absolute precepts of justice'.

single-common-good.rationale: Zapatismo spoke of one justice but also defended specific class interests of the peasantry; no clear position.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora return was never a concern of the movement and its principles give no answer.

economic-freedom.rationale: Zapatismo tied freedom to land ownership rather than to market freedom; the statement does not map onto its view.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The leaders were liberal laicists while followers were devout Catholics; no stated view.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The public-assistance law covered all human beings unable to work, without a citizenship test, but the question was never addressed directly.

class-collaboration.rationale: Leaders counted owners and workers alike as productive classes but backed strikes, boycotts and sabotage; the stance is mixed.

dominated-front.rationale: Zapata hoped for solidarity among oppressed peoples, but in class not national terms; no stated view on a front of states.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Zapata wrote that landlords held land through 'the force of armies and the iniquity of the laws', and the council called the army a tool to oppress the people.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The council discussed mining law and taxing foreign companies, but nothing on expanding oil or coal; no position.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The marriage law saw women as the weaker party needing legal protection, but there is no theory of systematic male advantage; neutral.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Plan of Ayala denounces Madero as a traitor allied with the old científicos, and the council required officials to be watched by the people and barred from enriching themselves.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Zapatista programme gave the state duties of land reform, labour protection, public assistance and free schooling, far beyond a minimal state.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The public-assistance law rejected charity as contrary to 'the equality of all men', and Zapata's letter speaks for all oppressed humanity.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Zapata praised the Russian revolution as humanity's cause but held no doctrine about socialism in one country.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Zapata compared foreign capital to Spanish colonial extraction but did not call Mexico a settler-colonial state; no clear position.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Montaño's education law made public primary schooling free and lay, though Ávila says laicism was the intellectuals' view rather than the base's.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Plan of Ayala condemns Madero for imposing governors on states against their will and calls for elected federal and state powers.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The Plan of Ayala authorises villages to seize lands held by hacendados and defend them by arms, plainly endorsing force to achieve justice.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Ávila concludes that Zapatismo wanted a state that attends first to the most numerous and unprotected classes.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Zapatista delegates forced the Convention programme to recognise strikes, boycotts and even sabotage as legitimate workers' weapons.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Zapata blamed poverty on the monopoly of land by 'a few powerful individuals', and Mendoza López on landlords' rent.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In wartime, justice was run by military chiefs, yet the programme guaranteed absolute press freedom; no stated position.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Zapatista press law guaranteed absolute freedom of expression without censorship, with disputes heard by popular juries.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Zapatista law limited officials' pay to what supports a family of the middle class and barred them from holding several posts.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The Plan of Ayala adopts the Plan of San Luis Potosí, whose principle was 'effective suffrage and no reelection', and attacks Madero for betraying it.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Mexico had no permanent military alliances; the question does not apply.

people-in-arms.rationale: The council's army law replaced the permanent army with the people in arms for national defence, never again a standing institution.

death-penalty.rationale: The Zapatista justice law abolished the death penalty for ever, although in wartime the movement shot traitors.

minority-language-support.rationale: Despite its Nahua base, the sources record no language policy; Montaño's education plan was national in scope.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Plan of Ayala breaks with Madero precisely because a political revolution without land reform was a betrayal; land was the cause of the revolution.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The Convention programme backed direct suffrage but also a parliamentary regime; how the head of state would be chosen is unclear.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Zapata called land 'the property of all, like water and air', and the Zapatista laws expropriated holdings that served monopoly rather than subsistence.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Plan of Ayala holds up Juárez's laws on ecclesiastical property, which confiscated Church wealth, as the model for its expropriations.

character-from-environment.rationale: The Zapatista justice law held society guilty for crime because it left most people in poverty, ignorance and neglect.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Plan of Ayala orders a third of the great estates expropriated to give ejidos and fields to villages, and the 1915 law went further in Morelos.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Zapata's letter speaks of an awakening of conscience as well as land; no materialist theory is stated.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The movement wanted plebiscites on laws but also independent popular juries; no clear view.

moral-incentives.rationale: The council stressed revolutionary morality for officials but promised workers the full product of their labour; no clear view on incentives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Zapatismo grew from village grievances into a mass peasant army; the foco theory question does not map onto it.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The movement wanted fundamental laws ratified by plebiscite but said nothing on entrenchment; no clear position.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The Plan of Ayala relies on colonial-era village land titles rather than voiding colonial acts; the question does not map.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Plan of Ayala provides for an interim president and then elections to federal and state powers.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Plan of Ayala withdraws recognition from Madero as president for betraying the revolution and violating the law and the people's will, and calls for his overthrow.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Zapatista delegates secured a parliamentary form of government in the Convention programme, the only time Mexico had one.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Zapatista law replaced charity with justice, calling charity degrading to human dignity, rather than relying on the duty of the rich.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Zapatismo gave absolute primacy to civil over military authority and wanted the permanent army abolished.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: The council's marriage law allowed divorce at the request of the parties, though Ávila says the base had expressed no such view.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Zapata called land the property of all, and the movement's motto was that land belongs to those who work it.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The colonisation law invited foreign settlers, yet the movement opposed foreign investment; the evidence pulls both ways.

local-production.rationale: Village subsistence farming was the base, but leaders also wanted production for wider markets; no clear view.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: No basis in the movement's tradition; it resented foreign domination, which grounds this inference.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The divorce law was meant to help women, but no link to economic transformation is stated.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Plan nationalised opponents' property and branded dissenting chiefs traitors, yet the programme guaranteed press freedom; the evidence pulls both ways.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Zapatista Morelos ran reform through municipal councils of elders and elected local reform boards, and laws were to be approved by plebiscite.

social-market-economy.rationale: The mixed economy described by historians resembles this, but with expropriation far beyond it; no clear position.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Zapatista intellectuals legislated to abolish the permanent army, keeping only an armed people for defence and police forces for order.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Zapata wrote that land monopolised by a few powerful individuals, backed by armies and laws, had kept peasants exploited for generations.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The public-assistance law criticised charity for degrading human dignity and replaced it with state assistance as a matter of justice.

term-limits.rationale: The movement upheld the revolutionary principle of no reelection that the Plan of Ayala accuses Madero of betraying.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Zapatista intellectuals called landlords an idle, harmful class appropriating rent and wanted every productive class to receive the full product of its work.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: An armed movement, Zapatismo told villages to defend recovered land by force of arms.

second-chamber.rationale: The Convention programme, shaped by Zapatista delegates, called for abolition of the Senate along with the vice-presidency.

municipal-property.rationale: The labour law put socialised industries in the patrimony of the municipality where they stood, run by workers' cooperatives, but this covered only some firms.

family-wage.rationale: The officials law tied public salaries to what supports an official and his family, and the agrarian law gave each person land enough for their family's subsistence.

person-over-state.rationale: The movement spoke of natural rights but also of collective revolutionary duties; no clear position.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The Zapatista army law replaced the permanent army with the people in arms, and villages were told to hold their land by arms.

farm-price-support.rationale: The Morelos reforms created credit unions and the agrarian law an agricultural bank to support farmers, though price guarantees are not mentioned.

premarital-sex.rationale: The marriage law recognised free unions, but the base was traditional; no clear position.

simple-living.rationale: Officials were to live modestly, but no general ideal of simple living is stated.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: A Zapatista council law ordered the immediate suppression of all taxes on the consumption of basic necessities.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Assistance targeted those unable to work, while schooling was universal; no clear position.

national-resource-control.rationale: The movement was strongly nationalist and opposed foreign investment in Morelos and Mexico.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The Zapatista public-assistance law made the state responsible for feeding, housing and caring for everyone unable to work, as a matter of justice rather than charity. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Land, water and woods taken from villages by large estates should be restored to the villages.
missingStatements.rationale: Restitution of usurped village lands under their old titles is the first demand of the Plan of Ayala and the core of the 1915 Agrarian Law.

missingStatements.text: There should be a legal upper limit on how much land any one person may own.
missingStatements.rationale: The 1915 Agrarian Law capped holdings at 100 to 1,000 hectares depending on land quality, to end the monopoly of land for good.

missingStatements.text: A country's permanent army should be abolished and replaced by the armed people.
missingStatements.rationale: The Zapatista council's army law abolished the standing army as an instrument of oppression and entrusted defence to the people in arms.

notes: Historians distinguish the Zapatista headquarters' pragmatic, village-centred rule from the national programme written by its intellectuals (Palafox, Montaño, Mendoza López, Zubiría, Amezcua); Ávila Espinosa argues the programme was broadly representative but flags gradual socialisation, cooperatives, laicism and the marriage law as the intellectuals' own views, so those answers are low confidence. Many modern questions are anachronistic for a 1910s agrarian movement and are marked low. The EZLN (neozapatismo) is audited separately.
